opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's actually a pretty rational strategy, and in some ways it mirrors what we see with the big American platforms. If you're Alibaba, ByteDance, Tencent, or Baidu, you have an enormous amount of distribution: users, cloud customers, apps with hundreds of millions of people in them. The model is becoming a core layer of the stack. If you don't own that layer, you're dependent on someone else for what could be the most important technology of the decade. So there's a strong defensive logic to it.

What's interesting about the Chinese ecosystem, though, is how much of it has leaned into open weights. Alibaba with Qwen is the clearest example. They've released a huge range of model sizes, very permissively, and iterated incredibly fast. From my seat working on open post-training research, Qwen models became the default base models a lot of academics and startups build on, including in the U.S. That's a big soft-power and ecosystem win that I don't think people fully appreciated at first. DeepSeek isn't a platform company, but it showed everyone that a relatively lean team with strong engineering could get near the frontier, and that put a lot of pressure on the big platforms to keep up.

The way I'd frame the strategy is roughly three things. First, they want a model good enough that they're not strategically dependent on anyone, especially given export controls and geopolitical uncertainty. Second, they use open releases to build developer mindshare and pull people toward their cloud and tooling, much as Meta tried to with Llama. Third, they have a real advantage in integration. ByteDance can put models into Doubao and Douyin and get feedback and usage at a scale very few labs have.

The challenges are real too. Compute is the big one. Export controls on advanced Nvidia chips mean they have to be much more efficient, and you see that in the architecture choices: mixture-of-experts, attention efficiency tricks, and very careful training recipes. In a way, the constraint has pushed some genuinely good research. But at the absolute frontier, scaling up RL and inference-time compute, having less compute does hurt, and they have to make harder trade-offs about what to train.

There's also a question of whether every big company needs its own frontier model, or whether the market consolidates. I suspect, like in the U.S., you'll see a few players at the top and many others who either fine-tune or fall back to using someone else's models. But for the largest platforms, I think building in-house is close to non-negotiable. The interesting part to watch is whether they keep releasing openly as they get closer to the frontier, or whether commercial pressure pushes them toward closing things up the way the American labs did.

r001.rationale: The response says large platforms have extensive distribution and that limited compute hurts frontier work, but it does not clearly connect AI’s resource dependence to an advantage for large companies.

r002.rationale: It gives reasons for investing in models, but does not describe returns from AI-improved products funding further AI investment.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention Ant, Bailing, Alipay, or Western observers’ puzzlement about their breadth of operations.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing to say is that it's not one strategy, it's several, and the companies are in very different positions. Alibaba with Qwen is the clearest case of a platform company deciding that the model itself is a strategic asset and going all the way to the frontier, or near it, and releasing openly. ByteDance is spending enormous amounts of money but has been much more product-oriented with Doubao, and until recently didn't lean as hard on open weights. Tencent and Baidu have been somewhere in between, and Baidu in particular has had a hard time holding onto the narrative even though they were early.

What ties them together is that these companies have the three things you actually need: they have cash flow from a core business that doesn't depend on the model, they have enormous distribution in the form of apps with hundreds of millions of users, and they have data and compute infrastructure already in place. That's the same structural advantage Google and Meta have in the US. So I'd push back a little on framing it as unusual. It's the default move for a platform company. The interesting question is why they're doing it the way they are.

And the way they're doing it, especially Alibaba, is open weights, and that's a deliberate choice that fits their situation. If you're a Chinese cloud provider, you're not going to win the global API business against OpenAI or Anthropic on brand or on trust. What you can do is make your model the one everyone builds on, so that when people fine-tune, when startups ship products, when researchers write papers, they're on your stack. Qwen has become the most downloaded, most fine-tuned family in the world by a good margin, and that's a real achievement that compounds. It also helps domestically, where the cloud business is the thing they actually monetize.

The second factor is export controls. When you can't count on buying the best chips, you get pushed toward efficiency, toward mixture-of-experts architectures, toward distillation, toward smaller models that run well. That's partly why these labs ended up so good at the cost side of the frontier, and DeepSeek obviously is the extreme example even though it's not a platform company.

Where I'm more skeptical is on the question of whether any of them will actually lead. The gap to the absolute frontier is real, I'd say somewhere in the range of six months to a year depending on how you measure, and the compute constraints make it hard to close. There's also a risk that spending at this level across four or five companies is just not rational for all of them. Some of these efforts will get consolidated or quietly deprioritized. And there's a political dimension where the state's priorities and the companies' priorities don't always line up.

But the big picture is that the platform companies, plus the labs like DeepSeek and Moonshot, have made China the center of gravity for open models. That matters enormously for the rest of the world, because the alternative for a developer who doesn't want to depend on a US closed API is increasingly a Chinese model. I don't think the US labs have fully reckoned with what that means yet.

r001.rationale: The response says platform companies have cash flow, enormous user distribution, and data and compute infrastructure, describing these as structural advantages for building AI models.

r002.rationale: It mentions Qwen adoption compounding and models supporting cloud monetization, but does not identify returns from AI-improved products funding further AI investment.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss Ant’s Bailing model, Western observers’ puzzlement, or Alipay’s breadth of operations and use cases.

astra-6.text:
I think it makes a lot of strategic sense, but I’d separate building a competitive model from trying to have the best model in the world. Those are very different investments.

If you’re a large platform company, you already have products, distribution, and infrastructure. Owning the model gives you more control over cost, latency, and how it fits into those products. You don’t necessarily need to win every benchmark for that to be valuable. You need a model that serves your users well at a price that makes sense.

The harder question is how much frontier research each company should fund. Training models is expensive, and keeping up requires repeated investment. There’s a risk of treating it as something you have to do because every competitor is doing it, without a clear connection to the business.

So I’d assess the strategy by looking at what happens after training: Can they turn the model into something people actually use? Can they improve it from that experience? For a platform company, that connection between the model and the product could matter much more than a brief lead on a leaderboard.

r001.rationale: The response says large platforms already have products, distribution, and infrastructure, and that training is expensive, but it does not state that AI’s resource demands favor large companies.

r002.rationale: It connects models to product use and improvement, but does not say returns from AI-improved products fund further AI investment.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention Ant’s Bailing model or explain Western observers’ puzzlement by reference to Alipay’s breadth.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it makes a lot of sense for them to build their own models, because they already have products, distribution, and infrastructure where those models can be useful. They don’t necessarily need to have the best model on every benchmark. They need a model that works well for their users and that they can serve economically.

The question is how much they should invest in pushing the frontier versus adapting models to their businesses. Those are different bets. If AI becomes a core part of search, commerce, or messaging, having control over the model gives you more flexibility over cost, latency, and the user experience. But owning a model isn’t a strategy by itself. You still have to turn that capability into something people want to use.

r001.rationale: The response mentions existing products, distribution, and infrastructure, but does not state that AI’s dependence on resources favors large companies.

r002.rationale: It discusses economic serving and model investment, but does not describe product returns funding further AI investment in a self-reinforcing cycle.

r003.rationale: It does not mention Ant, Bailing, Alipay, or Western observers’ lack of awareness of Alipay’s breadth.
